title: Lighting the Lamps, Setting Apart Helpers
overview: This chapter tells how the lamps in the sacred tent were first lit and how the tribe of Levi was cleansed and handed over to serve there.

parts.label: The lamps lit (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The sacred tent had no windows, so the seven lamps on the gold lampstand were its only light, set to shine on the space in front of it. Lighting them was the task of Aaron the high priest, and the lampstand was hammered from gold to match the design God had shown Moses.

parts.label: Cleansing the Levites (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: The Levites were the tribe chosen to help the priests, but being born into it was not enough; they first had to be made ritually fit. They were sprinkled with purifying water, shaved their whole bodies and washed their clothes, and two young bulls were brought for sacrifice.

parts.label: Handed over to God (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: The text says the Israelites laid hands on the Levites; since a whole nation could hardly do this, it may have been done through a smaller group such as leaders or firstborn sons, though that is a guess. The gesture seems to mean giving them to God on everyone's behalf, and Aaron then presented them as a "wave offering," a gift lifted up before God, while the bulls were sacrificed to make the Levites right with God.

parts.label: In place of the firstborn (vv. 14-19)
parts.note: Since the night the firstborn of Egypt died, Israel's firstborn sons were said to belong to God, and now the Levites take their place. Working at the sanctuary for the people, they were meant to keep disaster from striking when ordinary Israelites came near holy things.

parts.label: Done as commanded (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: Moses, Aaron and the people carried out every step. The Levites then began their work at the tent under the direction of Aaron and his sons.

parts.label: Starting and retiring ages (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: Levites began at twenty-five and stopped regular work at fifty, though older men could still help their younger colleagues. Another chapter gives thirty as the starting age; one common explanation is that the first five years were a kind of apprenticeship, but no one knows for sure.

think: When someone steps back from the work they spent years doing but stays on to help others, what do you think changes about their place in a community, and what stays the same?
